title: ITN 170 Linux Commands Study Guide
description: A command-line reference for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9: the shell, the filesystem, redirection and the text toolkit, users and groups, permissions, software, storage, processes and services, and networking and SSH.

blocks.text: The Shell Prompt
Bash is the default shell on RHEL 9. The prompt tells you three things before you type anything: who you are, which machine you are on, and where you are standing.

[student@servera ~]$      <- $ means an ordinary user
[root@servera ~]#        <- # means you are root: think before you press enter

blocks.label: Read the prompt:
blocks.text: The `~` is the current directory, written as a shortcut for your home. If it says `/etc`, you are in /etc. Most destructive accidents start with being somewhere you did not think you were.
The shape of a command

command  [options]  [arguments]

ls       -l -a      /etc
ls       -la        /etc          <- short options can be bundled
ls       --all      /etc          <- long options use two dashes

items: **Short options** are a single dash and one letter: `-l`. Several can be combined: `-la` is the same as `-l -a`.
**Long options** are two dashes and a word: `--all`. They are clearer in scripts, where somebody else has to read them later.
**Arguments** are what the command acts on. Most commands accept more than one.
Everything is **case-sensitive**: `ls` is a command, `LS` is not.

blocks.text: Editing the line you are typing

rows: Complete a command or filename; press twice to list the possibilities
Walk back and forward through your command history
Jump to the beginning / end of the line
Delete to the beginning / end of the line
Delete the word before the cursor
Clear the screen, keeping what you have typed
Abandon what is running, or what you are typing
End of input: logs you out of the shell
Search backwards through history for a command you ran before

blocks.label: Tab completion is a safety feature:
blocks.text: It is not only faster. If Tab does not complete a filename, the file is not there, or you are not where you think you are -- which is worth knowing before the command runs.
History

history            # numbered list of what you have run
!42                # run command number 42 again
!!                 # run the previous command again
sudo !!            # ... this time with sudo
!ls                # the most recent command starting with ls
Getting Help

rows: A quick summary of options. The first thing to try.
The full manual page: options, files, exit codes, examples
Search every manual page's description for a keyword
The same search under a different name
One line saying what a command is for
The path to the program that would actually run
Whether it is a builtin, an alias, or a program on disk
The GNU documentation, when a manual page is not enough

blocks.text: Reading a manual page

items: Inside `man`, **/** searches, **n** jumps to the next match, **q** quits. It is `less`, so all of `less`'s keys work.
**SYNOPSIS** shows the syntax. Square brackets mean optional, `...` means repeatable.
**EXAMPLES**, near the bottom, is usually the fastest part of the page.
Manual pages are in numbered sections. `man 5 passwd` is the **file format** /etc/passwd; `man 1 passwd` is the **command**.

blocks.text: One Tree, No Drive Letters
Everything on a Linux system hangs off a single root directory, `/`. Extra disks do not get a letter -- they are **mounted** onto a directory somewhere in that one tree.

rows: The root user's home directory -- not the same as /
Data that changes: logs, spools, caches
Log files, including the ones you read when something breaks
Temporary files; world-writable and periodically cleaned out
A view of the running kernel and its processes, generated on the fly
Conventional places to mount other filesystems
The kernel and what is needed to start the machine

blocks.text: Paths

rows: An **absolute** path: start at root, no matter where you are
A **relative** path: start from the current directory
With `cd`, the directory you were in before

blocks.text:
pwd                 # where am I?
cd /var/log         # absolute: works from anywhere
cd ..               # up one level
cd ../..            # up two
cd ~                # home
cd                  # also home
cd -                # back to where I just was

blocks.label: Absolute or relative?
blocks.text: Use absolute paths in scripts and in anything destructive, because they mean the same thing wherever they run. Use relative paths interactively, where you can see the prompt.
Listing

rows: Long format: permissions, links, owner, group, size, date
Everything, including names beginning with a dot
Both at once -- the everyday listing
Sizes as K, M and G rather than bytes
Oldest first, so the newest ends up next to your prompt
The directory itself, not what is inside it
Include the inode number of each entry

blocks.label: Hidden files:
blocks.text: There is no hidden attribute. A file is hidden simply because its name begins with a dot, and `ls -a` shows it. That is the whole mechanism.
Reading files without editing them

cat file            # print the whole thing
less file           # page through it; / searches, q quits
head file           # first 10 lines
head -3 file        # first 3
tail file           # last 10 lines
tail -f /var/log/messages   # follow it as it grows
file something      # what kind of file is this?
wc -l file          # how many lines?
Creating, Copying, Moving, Removing

rows: Create an empty file, or update the timestamps of one that exists
Create a whole path, making parents as needed
Copy a directory and everything in it
Rename, or move into another directory -- the same command
Delete a file. There is no recycle bin.
Delete a directory and its contents
Delete a directory only if it is already empty

blocks.label: There is no undo:
blocks.text: `rm` does not ask and does not keep a copy. Two habits prevent nearly every accident: run the pattern through `ls` first to see what it matches, and check `pwd` before deleting anything.
Links

ln  original.txt  hardlink.txt     # hard link: a second name for one inode
ln -s original.txt softlink.txt    # symbolic link: a signpost holding a path

rows: Another name for the same inode
A small file holding a path
Still works -- data goes when the last name does

blocks.text: Shell Expansions
The shell rewrites your line **before** the command runs. The command never sees the pattern -- only the result. This is why `ls **.txt` and `rm **.txt` match exactly the same files.

rows: Any run of characters, including none
One character, not from that set
**Brace expansion**: generates one word per item, whether or not any file matches

blocks.text:
touch report{1,2,3}.txt         # creates three files
touch page{01..05}.php          # creates five
ls report?.txt                  # report1.txt ... report5.txt
ls *.{txt,php}                  # both extensions
echo *.txt                      # preview what a pattern expands to

blocks.label: The one real difference:
blocks.text: Globs (`*`, `?`, `[...]`) only produce names that exist. Brace expansion generates text whether the files exist or not -- which is exactly why it works with `touch` and `mkdir`.
Quoting

rows: Stops globbing and word splitting; `$VAR` and `$(cmd)` are still expanded
The next single character is literal

blocks.text:
touch "my file.txt"      # one file, with a space in the name
touch my\ file.txt       # the same thing
echo "$HOME"             # /home/student
echo '$HOME'             # $HOME
Variables and substitution

echo $HOME $USER $PATH $PWD
echo "Today is $(date)"        # command substitution
name="report"                  # no spaces around the =
echo "${name}1.txt"            # braces separate the name from what follows
Loops

for f in *.txt; do cp "$f" "$f.bak"; done
for i in {1..3}; do mkdir "site-$i"; done

blocks.label: Quote the variable:
blocks.text: `"$f"` keeps a filename with a space in it as one argument. Unquoted, `spaced name.txt` becomes two arguments and the command does the wrong thing.
vim, in the Five Minutes You Need
vim opens in **command mode**, where letters are commands rather than text. `vi` is guaranteed to exist on any RHEL system, which is why it is worth knowing even if you prefer `nano`.

rows: Open a new line below and insert
Back to command mode -- always safe to press
Quit and throw away the changes

blocks.text: nano, which is the one that opens here

nano shows its commands along the bottom of the screen, so there is nothing to memorise before you start. `^` means Ctrl. It is friendlier than vim and usually installed — but **usually** is the catch, which is why vim is still worth knowing.

rows: Write Out — save; it asks for the filename, Enter confirms
Exit — if the buffer changed it asks whether to save first
Cut the current line / paste it back
Read File — insert another file at the cursor
Cur Pos — which line, column and character you are on

blocks.label: In the practice terminal:
blocks.text: `nano` really opens — in the Practice Terminal and on every lab page. Saving goes through the machine's permissions, so a file you may not write refuses to save, exactly as it would on a real system. `vim` does not run in the browser; the keystrokes above the streams section are what you need for it.
The Three Streams
All three point at your terminal by default, which is why output and errors look like one thing. They are not, and `>` only moves stdout.

rows: stdout to the file, then stderr to the same place
A here document: the following lines, until END alone

blocks.label: Order matters:
blocks.text: `> file 2>&1` works; `2>&1 > file` does not. The second one copies stderr to where stdout points **at that moment** -- still the terminal -- and only then moves stdout.
Pipes

ls -a | wc -l                       # count the entries
grep 404 access.log | tail -3       # filter, then trim
sort fruit.txt | uniq -c            # group, then count
ps aux | grep sshd                  # find a process
sort fruit.txt | tee sorted.txt     # save a copy and keep going

items: A pipe connects the **stdout** of the left command to the **stdin** of the right one. Errors are not piped.
A redirection at the end of a pipeline belongs to the **last** command in it.
`tee` writes to a file **and** passes the data along; `tee -a` appends.

blocks.text: The Text Toolkit
grep -- find lines

rows: Invert: print the lines that do **not** match
Count matching lines instead of printing them
Print only the names of files that matched
Match whole words only -- `ssh` no longer matches `sshd`

blocks.text:
grep -v '^#' /etc/services         # drop the comments
grep -c 404 access.log             # how many
grep -rn mysql /etc                # where, and on which line
grep '^root' /etc/passwd           # ^ anchors to the start, $ to the end

blocks.label: Quote the pattern:
blocks.text: Single quotes stop the shell expanding `*`, `?` and `$` before grep sees them.
cut, sort, uniq, tr, wc

cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd            # first colon-separated field
cut -d, -f2,6 employees.csv        # two comma-separated fields

sort file                          # alphabetical
sort -n numbers.txt                # numeric: 9 before 115
sort -rn numbers.txt               # biggest first
sort -u file                       # sorted, duplicates removed

sort file | uniq -c                # count each distinct line
sort file | uniq -d                # only the duplicated ones

tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < file              # translate; reads stdin only
tr -d ' ' < file                   # delete characters

wc file                            # lines, words, characters
wc -l file

blocks.label: Why sort before uniq:
blocks.text: `uniq` only compares a line with the one immediately before it. Sorting is what puts the identical lines next to each other.
sed -- edit a stream

sed 's/old/new/'  file      # first match on each line
sed 's/old/new/g' file      # every match
sed -i 's/old/new/g' file   # edit the file in place
sed -i.bak 's/a/b/g' file   # ... keeping file.bak
sed -n '4p' file            # print only line 4
sed -n '2,5p' file          # lines 2 to 5
sed '/^#/d' file            # delete the comment lines

blocks.label: Preview first:
blocks.text: Run it without `-i` and read the output. Then add `-i`. On anything under /etc, use `-i.bak`.
awk -- work with columns

awk '{print $1, $3}'  inventory.txt          # first and third columns
awk '{print $NF}'     hosts.txt              # the last column
awk -F, '{print $2}'  employees.csv          # comma-separated
awk -F, '$3=="Support" {print $2}' employees.csv
awk 'NR != 1 {total += $3} END {print total}' inventory.txt
awk '$5 > 1000'       access.log             # print lines matching a condition

rows: The number of fields, so `$NF` is the last one
Blocks that run before the first line / after the last

blocks.label: Which tool?
blocks.text: **grep** picks lines. **cut** takes fixed columns. **sed** changes text. **awk** does anything involving a condition on a column, or arithmetic.
Who Am I?

whoami                 # just the name
id                     # uid, primary group, every supplementary group
id operator1           # the same, for somebody else
groups                 # the groups I am in
who / w                # who is logged in right now
The Account Files

rows: Account name, UID, GID, comment, home, shell
Group names, GIDs and supplementary members
The defaults applied to new accounts

blocks.text:
student:x:1000:1000:Student User:/home/student:/bin/bash
   1     2   3    4        5             6            7

1 name   2 password placeholder (x = see /etc/shadow)   3 UID
4 primary GID   5 comment (GECOS)   6 home   7 login shell

rows: Regular users created by an administrator

blocks.label: /sbin/nologin
blocks.text: An account with that shell is valid -- it owns files and runs processes -- but nobody can log in as it. That is how service accounts are locked down.
Creating and Changing Accounts

sudo useradd analyst                       # defaults for everything
sudo useradd -c 'Data Analyst' analyst     # set the comment
sudo useradd -u 1500 webops                # fix the UID
sudo useradd -s /sbin/nologin backupsvc    # a service account
sudo useradd -G operators newperson        # with a supplementary group

sudo usermod -c 'New Name' analyst
sudo usermod -s /bin/bash backupsvc
sudo usermod -L analyst                    # lock / -U unlock
sudo userdel analyst                       # keep the home directory
sudo userdel -r analyst                    # remove it too
Groups

sudo groupadd webadmin
sudo groupadd -g 10500 auditors
sudo groupdel webadmin

sudo usermod -aG operators dbadmin     # ADD to supplementary groups
sudo usermod -g consultants operator3  # change the primary group
getent group techdocs                  # who is in it

blocks.label: The -a is not optional:
blocks.text: `usermod -G operators dbadmin` **replaces** every supplementary group the account had -- including `wheel`, which is how someone loses sudo by accident. Always `-aG`, and always run `id user` first so you know what to put back.

items: A user has exactly **one primary group**, recorded in /etc/passwd. New files they create get that group.
A user can have **any number of supplementary groups**, recorded in /etc/group. These only grant access.
Group changes do not apply to a session that is already open. Log out and back in, or start a new login shell.

blocks.text: Passwords and Aging

sudo passwd analyst        # set a password
passwd                     # change my own
sudo passwd -l operator2   # lock  /  -u unlock
sudo passwd -S operator2   # status in one line

sudo chage -l operator1    # show the aging settings
sudo chage -d 0 dbadmin    # must change password at next login
sudo chage -M 90 dbadmin   # maximum password age
sudo chage -E 2026-06-30 contractor   # the account itself expires
Becoming root

rows: A full login shell as root: their environment, their home. Needs the **root** password.
root's identity, but your environment and current directory
One command as root. Needs **your own** password.
An interactive root shell, authenticated as you

blocks.label: Why sudo wins:
blocks.text: Each administrator uses their own password, every command is logged with their name, access is removed by taking them out of a group, and rules can allow specific commands rather than everything. On RHEL, membership of **wheel** is what grants it. Edit the rules with **visudo**, never a plain editor -- it refuses to save a file it cannot parse.
Reading a Long Listing

-rw-r--r--  1  student  student   22  Jun  4 18:15  public.txt
│└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘  │     │        │       │        │           │
│ │  │  │   │     │        │       │        │           └ name
│ │  │  │   │     │        │       │        └ last modified
│ │  │  │   │     │        │       └ size in bytes
│ │  │  │   │     │        └ group
│ │  │  │   │     └ owner
│ │  │  │   └ link count
│ │  │  └ other:  what everyone else may do
│ │  └ group:   what members of the group may do
│ └ user:    what the owner may do
└ type: - file, d directory, l symlink, b block, c character
What the Bits Mean

rows: Enter it and reach things by name

blocks.label: The one that catches everyone:
blocks.text: Deleting a file needs **write permission on the directory**, not on the file. And without **x** on a directory you cannot reach anything inside it, however open the files themselves are.
chmod
Octal: set all three columns at once

chmod 644 file      # rw-r--r--   the usual file
chmod 640 file      # rw-r-----   owner writes, team reads
chmod 600 file      # rw-------   private
chmod 755 dir       # rwxr-xr-x   the usual directory
chmod 700 dir       # rwx------   private directory
chmod -R 700 dir    # and everything inside it
Symbolic: change only what you name

chmod u+x script.sh     # add execute for the owner
chmod go-w file         # remove write from group and other
chmod a+r file          # everyone can read
chmod g=r file          # group becomes exactly read
chmod g= file           # group gets nothing

blocks.label: Which form?
blocks.text: Octal when you want a known end state. Symbolic when you want to change one thing and leave the rest alone. Only the owner and root may run chmod at all.
Ownership

sudo chown operator1 file            # change the owner
sudo chown operator1:operators file  # owner and group
sudo chown :operators file           # group only
chgrp techdocs file                  # group only, no sudo needed
                                     #   if you own it and are in the group
sudo chown -R apache:apache /var/www # a whole tree
Only root may give a file to another **user** -- otherwise anyone could dodge a quota by handing their files away. You may give a file to a **group** you already belong to.
The umask

umask               # show it: 0022
umask 007           # set it for this shell

New files start from 666 and new directories from 777.
The umask bits are then removed:

  666 - 022 = 644     rw-r--r--
  777 - 022 = 755     rwxr-xr-x
  666 - 007 = 660     rw-rw----

blocks.label: Why a new script is never executable:
blocks.text: Files start from 666, which has no execute bit to begin with. That is why you always have to `chmod +x` a script you just wrote.
Special Permissions

rows: Runs as the file's owner, not as whoever started it
New entries inherit the directory's group
Only an entry's owner may delete it

blocks.text:
drwxrwsr-x   <- s in the GROUP execute position: setgid
-rwsr-xr-x   <- s in the USER  execute position: setuid (this is /usr/bin/passwd)
drwxrwxrwt   <- t at the end: sticky (this is /tmp)

chmod g+s  shared/      or  chmod 2775 shared/
chmod +t   dropbox/     or  chmod 1777 dropbox/

blocks.label: A shared team directory:
blocks.text: `chmod 2770` plus a group everyone is in. The **2** makes every file created inside inherit the team group, without which the group permission bits never apply to anyone's files. Add the sticky bit (**3770**) if members should not be able to delete each other's work.
Diagnosing Permission Denied

items: `ls -l thefile` -- the mode, the owner and the group. Which column applies to this user?
`id theuser` -- their UID and every group. A membership added since they logged in is not in their current session.
Every directory on the path needs **x**. `namei -l /full/path/to/file` checks all of them at once.
Still stuck? A trailing `.` or `+` on the mode in `ls -l` means SELinux context or an ACL is involved.

blocks.text: rpm or dnf?

rows: One package, and the local database
Checks, but will not fetch them

blocks.text: dnf calls rpm to do the actual work. The split is 'fetch and resolve' versus 'ask and inspect'.
Reading a Package Name

tree  -  1.8.0  -  10  .  el9  .  x86_64  .rpm
  │        │        │       │       │
  │        │        │       │       └ architecture (noarch = any)
  │        │        │       └ built for RHEL 9
  │        │        └ release: which build of that version
  │        └ upstream version
  └ package name
Querying with rpm

rows: What is installed on this system?
Which of its files are configuration?
Which package does this file belong to?
The same questions, about a downloaded .rpm

blocks.label: Every query starts with -q:
blocks.text: rpm **with** -q asks questions. rpm **without** -q changes the system. That is the safest way to remember it.
Searching and Installing with dnf

dnf search tree                  # by name and summary
dnf provides /usr/bin/awk        # which package would give me this file?
dnf info httpd                   # details, installed or not
dnf list installed               # what is on the system
dnf list available               # what could be
dnf repolist                     # which repositories are enabled

sudo dnf install -y tree         # install, answering yes
sudo dnf remove -y nano          # remove
sudo dnf update -y               # update everything (= upgrade)
dnf check-update                 # what *would* be updated

dnf history                      # past transactions
sudo dnf history undo last       # reverse the most recent one

blocks.label: 'command not found' has a recipe:
blocks.text: `dnf provides /usr/bin/thecommand` names the package. Then `sudo dnf install <package>`, and confirm with `rpm -q`.
Groups and modules

dnf group list
sudo dnf group install "Development Tools"

dnf module list                  # streams and profiles
sudo dnf module enable php:8.0
A **group** is a named bundle of packages. A **module** is how RHEL 9 offers several versions of the same application; only one stream of a module can be enabled at a time.
Flatpak

flatpak list                     # installed applications
flatpak remotes                  # configured sources, e.g. flathub
flatpak search gimp
sudo flatpak install flathub org.gimp.GIMP

items: A Flatpak application **bundles its own dependencies** and runs sandboxed.
It has its own inventory: `rpm -qa` will never list it.
The trade: it can use a newer library than the system ships, at the cost of disk space and of not being covered by the system's own updates.

blocks.label: Repositories and subscriptions:
blocks.text: Repository definitions live in **/etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo**. On RHEL, which repositories appear at all depends on the subscription attached to the machine -- `subscription-manager status` is the first thing to check when `dnf install` finds nothing.
find -- walk the tree, live

find ~/labs -name '*.csv'                  # by name (quote the pattern!)
find ~/labs -iname '*.CSV'                 # ignoring case
find ~/labs -type f -name '*.txt'          # regular files only
find ~/labs -type d -name 'day-*'          # directories only
find /home -user operator1                 # by owner
find /var -size +100M                      # larger than 100 MB
find /etc -mtime -7                        # changed in the last week
find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null             # every setuid program
find ~/labs -type f -exec wc -l {} \;      # run a command on each result

rows: By name, with or without case
Modified within 7 days / more than 30 days ago
Run a command on each result (`+` batches them)

blocks.label: find vs locate:
blocks.text: **find** walks the filesystem and is always current. **locate** reads an index built by `updatedb` -- instant, but blind to anything created since. And locate only matches on the path: any search on size, time, owner or permissions has to be find.
Space

df -h                   # free space per filesystem
df -i                   # inode usage -- check this when df -h looks fine
du -sh ~/labs/survey    # total for one directory
du -sh *                # which subdirectory is eating the disk?
du -h --max-depth=1 /var

blocks.label: When df and du disagree:
blocks.text: `df` asks the filesystem; `du` adds up the files it can see. A deleted file still held open by a process is invisible to du but still counted by df -- which is why restarting the process suddenly frees the space. `lsof +L1` finds them.
Block Devices and Mounting

lsblk                        # disks and partitions as a tree
sudo blkid                   # type, LABEL and UUID of each device
mount                        # what is mounted right now
findmnt                      # the same, as a readable tree

sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt    # attach a filesystem
sudo umount /mnt             # detach it

cat /etc/fstab               # what gets mounted at boot
sudo mount -a                # test fstab without rebooting

items: **/etc/fstab** should refer to a filesystem by **UUID**, not by `/dev/sdb1`: device names can change when hardware is added.
Mounting **hides** whatever was already in the mount point directory. It comes back when you unmount.
'target is busy' on umount means a process has a file open there -- often your own shell. `lsof /mnt` or `fuser -m /mnt` names it.
RHEL 9 uses **xfs** for / and /boot by default.

blocks.text: Archives and Compression

tar -cf  archive.tar  dir/       # create
tar -czf archive.tar.gz dir/     # create, gzip-compressed
tar -tf  archive.tar             # list, without extracting
tar -xf  archive.tar             # extract
tar -xzf archive.tar.gz -C /tmp  # extract somewhere specific

gzip file        # replaces file with file.gz
gzip -k file     # keeps the original too
gunzip file.gz   # back again
zcat file.gz     # read it without unpacking

rows: Create / extract / list -- pick exactly one
Report each file as it goes

blocks.label: Two tools, one job:
blocks.text: `gzip` compresses **one file**. `tar` packs a directory into one file. That is why they are used together -- and why `tar -tf` before `tar -xf` is a good habit: an archive that unpacks into the current directory makes a mess.
Looking at Processes

ps                # just my terminal's processes
ps aux            # everything, BSD style: USER %CPU %MEM RSS STAT
ps -ef            # everything, UNIX style: includes PPID
pgrep -l sshd     # PIDs of processes by name
top               # live, refreshing view
top -bn1          # one plain snapshot, for a script
uptime            # load averages
free -h           # memory and swap

rows: R running, S sleeping, T stopped, Z zombie
Its terminal, or `?` for a daemon

items: A **zombie** has finished but its exit status has not been collected. It uses no CPU or memory and cannot be killed -- it is already dead.
An **orphan** is adopted by PID 1, systemd, which collects its status.
The load averages are for one, five and fifteen minutes. Compare them with the number of cores.

blocks.text: Jobs

sleep 300 &      # start in the background
jobs             # list this shell's jobs
fg %1            # bring job 1 to the foreground
bg %1            # let a suspended job carry on in the background
Ctrl+Z           # suspend the foreground job
Ctrl+C           # interrupt it

blocks.label: Jobs belong to the shell:
blocks.text: Close the terminal and the jobs go with it, unless they were started with `nohup` or disowned. Job numbers (`%1`) are per shell; PIDs are system-wide.
Signals

rows: Shut down cleanly. **The default.** Can be handled.
Stop now. Cannot be caught or ignored.
The terminal has gone; many daemons reread their config instead

blocks.text:
kill 1234          # SIGTERM -- ask nicely
kill -9 1234       # SIGKILL -- last resort
kill -HUP 1234     # reload configuration
killall httpd      # by program name
pkill -u operator1 # by pattern or by user

blocks.label: Ask, wait, then insist:
blocks.text: TERM first, so the process can flush buffers, close database connections and remove its lock files. `kill -9` skips all of that -- which is how you end up with a stale PID file that stops the service restarting.
systemd and systemctl

systemd is PID 1: the first process started at boot, and the thing that starts and supervises everything else. What it manages is described by **units** -- services, sockets, timers, mounts and targets.

systemctl status crond               # running? enabled? recent log lines
systemctl is-active sshd             # one word, useful exit status
systemctl is-enabled sshd
systemctl list-units --type=service   # what is loaded
systemctl list-unit-files             # everything installed

sudo systemctl start   httpd         # now
sudo systemctl stop    httpd
sudo systemctl restart httpd         # stop and start
sudo systemctl reload  httpd         # reread config, keep connections
sudo systemctl enable  httpd         # at boot
sudo systemctl disable httpd
sudo systemctl enable --now httpd    # both at once

journalctl -u httpd                  # this unit's log
journalctl -u httpd -b               # ... this boot only
journalctl -f                        # follow it live

blocks.label: start ≠ enable:
blocks.text: **start** runs it now. **enable** makes it start at boot. Neither implies the other, and forgetting `enable` is the classic reason a working service is gone after a reboot. `systemctl status` shows both: **Active** answers 'now?', and **Loaded** answers 'at boot?'.
Looking at the Network

ip addr show           # addresses on every interface (ip a)
ip addr show ens3      # just one interface
ip route               # the routing table, including the default gateway
hostname               # what this machine calls itself
hostnamectl            # hostname plus OS, kernel, virtualization
cat /etc/hosts         # local name-to-address map, checked before DNS

ping 172.25.250.11     # does the host answer?
ss -tlnp               # which TCP ports are listening, and what holds them
dig example.com        # what DNS says
host example.com

rows: Where traffic for other networks goes
What turns a name into an address
The name this machine calls itself

blocks.label: /24 means:
blocks.text: The first 24 bits are the network, leaving 8 bits for hosts -- the same as netmask 255.255.255.0. Anything from 172.25.250.1 to .254 is local and reached directly; everything else goes via the gateway.
NetworkManager

nmcli connection show               # the configured profiles
nmcli device status                 # the devices, and whether connected
sudo nmcli connection modify ens3 ipv4.addresses 172.25.250.10/24
sudo nmcli connection modify ens3 ipv4.method manual
sudo nmcli connection up ens3       # apply it

blocks.label: ip vs nmcli:
blocks.text: `ip addr add` changes only the running kernel, and NetworkManager or a reboot throws it away. Use `ip` to look and to test; use `nmcli connection modify` to make it stick. Interface names like **ens3** describe where the card sits on the bus, so they do not shuffle when hardware changes.
The Firewall

firewall-cmd --list-all                          # the active zone
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

**firewalld** organises rules into zones and is configured with **firewall-cmd**. Without `--permanent` a rule disappears at the next reload; with it, the rule is written but does not take effect until you `--reload`. Doing both is the normal pattern.
SSH

ssh serverb                       # log in as my own username
ssh operator1@serverb             # as someone else
ssh operator1@serverb hostname    # run one command and return

scp file.txt operator1@serverb:/tmp/     # push a file
scp operator1@serverb:/tmp/file.txt .    # pull one
sftp operator1@serverb                   # interactive transfer
Key-based authentication

ssh-keygen -t rsa                 # creates ~/.ssh/id_rsa and id_rsa.pub
ssh-copy-id operator1@serverb     # appends the PUBLIC key on the far end
ssh operator1@serverb             # no password needed now

rows: Your **private** key. Never leaves this machine. Mode 600.
Your public key -- the half you hand out
On the server: the public keys allowed to log in as this user
Host keys of servers you have connected to before

blocks.text: The server issues a random challenge; the client signs it with the private key and the server verifies the signature against the public key it already holds. **The private key is never transmitted**, which is why key authentication beats even a strong password -- there is nothing on the wire to capture, and nothing shared to guess.

blocks.label: Two warnings worth understanding:
blocks.text: **Permissions too open** on ~/.ssh or a key file makes sshd refuse it and fall back to asking for a password. **REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED** means the host key does not match known_hosts: usually a rebuilt server, but it is also exactly what an interception looks like -- verify before you delete the old entry.

blocks.label: Hardening:
blocks.text: `PermitRootLogin no` and `PasswordAuthentication no` in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, with keys for everyone who needs access. Administrators then log in as themselves and use sudo -- so the logs name a person.
Working Outward: a Troubleshooting Order

items: **Does the machine have the right address?** `ip addr show`
**Can it reach beyond its own subnet?** `ip route`, then ping the gateway
**Is the service running?** `systemctl status`, then `journalctl -u`
**Is it listening where you expect?** `ss -tlnp` -- bound to 127.0.0.1 serves only the machine itself
**Is the firewall letting it through?** `firewall-cmd --list-all`
**Is it a name problem?** If the address works and the name does not, look at DNS and /etc/hosts

blocks.label: Why this order:
blocks.text: Each step rules out everything below it. Guessing in the middle is what makes network troubleshooting take all afternoon.
